entries.author: Arx
entries.title: The Council of Chalcedon Defines Christ's Two Natures and Splits the Eastern Churches
entries.dek: In 451 more than 520 bishops meet at Chalcedon, across the Bosporus from Constantinople, and declare Christ one person in two natures. The churches of Egypt, Syria and Armenia refuse the formula.

pair.left: Pope Leo I and the council's bishops argued that Christ is one person acknowledged in two natures, divine and human, without confusion or division, fully God and fully human.
pair.right: Dioscorus's followers in Egypt and Syria argued, with Cyril, that Christ has one incarnate nature of God the Word, and that 'in two natures' conceded too much to Nestorius.

reading.label: The Stakes
reading.text: Both camps confessed Christ fully God and fully human; at stake was whose formula, and whose sees, Rome and Constantinople or Alexandria, would define orthodoxy for the empire's church.

entries.author: Arx
entries.title: Qin's First Emperor Orders the Books Burned
entries.dek: In 213 BC the chancellor Li Si persuades the First Emperor to burn private copies of the Odes, the Documents and rival states' histories. Historians still argue over how much burned.

pair.left: Chunyu Yue said no state had lasted long without taking antiquity as its teacher, and urged the emperor to give fiefs to his sons and brothers.
pair.right: Li Si said times had changed, that scholars studied the past to criticize the present and confuse the people, and that their books should burn.

reading.label: The Stakes
reading.text: Each man said he was guarding the dynasty; at stake was who could judge the emperor's rule, scholars reading old books or officials teaching the new law.

pair.right: Sergei Lavrov said the West had "tossed out all their principles" and called the freeze "nothing but theft."

reading.label: The Stakes
reading.text: Each side says it defends the rules; at stake is whether a state's reserves held abroad stay its own once it goes to war.

entries.author: Arx
entries.title: Turkey Turns Hagia Sophia Back into a Mosque
entries.dek: On 10 July 2020 a Turkish court voided the museum status and Erdogan ordered the former Byzantine cathedral reopened as a mosque, reversing the 1934 conversion.

pair.left: Ankara and the Presidency of Religious Affairs framed the reopening as lawful sovereign control and as continuity with the building's Ottoman use as a mosque.
pair.right: UNESCO, Orthodox churches, and secular critics framed the reopening as a break with shared heritage and with the 1934 museum settlement.

reading.label: The Stakes
reading.text: Both sides framed a claim to the same building. At stake is who controls Hagia Sophia: the Turkish state, through the Presidency of Religious Affairs, or the 1934 museum settlement held as shared heritage.

entries.author: Arx
entries.title: Britain and Russia Split Persia into Spheres and End the Great Game
entries.dek: On 31 August 1907 the two empires sign a convention in St Petersburg that divides Persia into a Russian north, a British southeast and a neutral middle. Tehran is not consulted.

pair.left: Grey and Izvolsky said the deal settled their Asian quarrels by agreement, and its text pledged to respect Persia's integrity and independence and equal trade for all nations.
pair.right: Persia's government said a pact signed without it threatened the country's integrity and refused to recognize it; nationalists who had looked to Britain turned against it.

reading.label: The Stakes
reading.text: Both empires spoke of peace and order in Asia; at stake was who would hold Persia's concessions, customs revenue and roads toward India: the two powers or the Persians.

entries.author: Arx
entries.title: Thirty-Nine Delegates Sign the US Constitution in Philadelphia
entries.dek: On 17 September 1787 the Philadelphia Convention signs a charter for a stronger national government and sends it to the states, opening the fight between Federalists and Anti-Federalists.

pair.left: Federalists such as Madison said a Congress that could not tax risked national bankruptcy and break-up, and that a large republic with a stronger national government would check faction.
pair.right: Anti-Federalists led by Patrick Henry said the charter would erode state sovereignty and individual liberty, that the presidency could grow into a monarchy, and that it lacked a bill of rights.

reading.label: The Stakes
reading.text: Both sides claimed the Revolution's legacy; at stake was whether the power to tax, regulate trade and make war would sit with a national government or stay with the states.

entries.author: Arx
entries.title: Hobbes Publishes Leviathan and Makes the Case for an Undivided Sovereign
entries.dek: In 1651, as England's civil wars end, Thomas Hobbes publishes Leviathan in London, arguing that only one undivided sovereign power can keep people from a war of all against all.

pair.left: Hobbes argued that without a common power people live in a war of every man against every man, so they must give one undivided sovereign their obedience for as long as it can protect them.
pair.right: Republicans such as James Harrington argued that a free state is an empire of laws, not of men, and Anglicans such as Bishop John Bramhall argued that his materialism led toward atheism.

reading.label: The Stakes
reading.text: Both camps wanted an end to civil war; at stake was whether peace required one undivided power over Church and state, or rule bound by law and by the Church's own authority.

entries.author: Arx
entries.title: Zemsky Sobor Elects 16-Year-Old Michael Romanov Tsar
entries.dek: On 3 March 1613 an assembly of the realm, meeting in the Kremlin after the Poles were driven out, chooses Michael Romanov as tsar and ends the Time of Troubles.

pair.left: Romanov-era and Soviet historians said the Sobor chose freely, voicing the wish of most Russians, and turned to a kinsman of Feodor I, the last tsar of the old line.
pair.right: Critics said Cossacks in Moscow forced Michael on boyars who had left him off their list, and that his backers wanted a young tsar they could steer.

reading.label: The Stakes
reading.text: Both sides trace the Romanov throne to 1613; at stake is whether it rested on the consent of the land, or on Cossack pressure and a boyar bet on a pliant boy.

entries.author: Arx
entries.title: Moscow Gets a Patriarch and Calls Itself the Third Rome
entries.dek: In 1589 the patriarch of Constantinople installs Job as Moscow's first patriarch, in a charter that names Russia the Third Rome. In 2018 the two churches split over Kyiv.

pair.left: In 2018 Moscow's Holy Synod said Constantinople's Ukraine decisions were an "encroachment on someone else's canonical regions" and broke communion with it.
pair.right: In 2018 Constantinople's Holy Synod said the 1686 letter letting Moscow ordain Kyiv's metropolitan was "issued for the circumstances of that time" and revoked it.

reading.label: The Stakes
reading.text: Both churches cite old charters; at stake is who ranks first in Orthodoxy, and whether the church in Kyiv answers to Moscow or stands on its own.

entries.author: Arx
entries.title: Bodin Publishes Six Books of the Commonwealth and Defines Sovereignty
entries.dek: In 1576, during France's wars of religion, Jean Bodin publishes Six Books of the Commonwealth in Paris and defines sovereignty as absolute and perpetual power to make law, still bound by God and the law of nature.

pair.left: Bodin argued that sovereignty is absolute and perpetual power to give law without the subjects' consent, that magistrates only hold it in deposit, and that the law of God and of nature still binds the sovereign.
pair.right: François Hotman and Théodore de Bèze argued that the Estates held authority over the making of a king and over public law, and that they could restrain or depose a king who ruled as a tyrant.

reading.label: The Stakes
reading.text: Both camps claimed a lawful authority to settle who commands; at stake was whether the power to make law and to judge a king sat with a sovereign, or with the Estates.

entries.author: Arx
entries.title: Mehmed II Makes the Anti-Union Monk Gennadios Patriarch
entries.dek: On 6 January 1454 the sultan who took Constantinople installs its leading foe of union with Rome as patriarch. Later sultans repeat the investiture for the patriarchs after him.

pair.left: Gennadios told the people of Constantinople that by forsaking their faith and trusting the Italians instead of God, they would lose their city.
pair.right: Bessarion said he urged union with Rome because he found no error in Latin doctrine, and would have suffered the worst before counseling it out of fear for the body.

reading.label: The Stakes
reading.text: Each side said it defended the true faith; at stake was who would protect and govern the Orthodox once Byzantium fell, a patriarch under the sultan or a Church joined to Rome.

entries.author: Arx
entries.title: Ibn Khaldun Writes the Muqaddimah, a Theory of How Dynasties Rise and Fall
entries.dek: In retreat at a fortress in the hills of western Algeria, a North African statesman drafts an introduction to world history that explains why ruling houses rise and fall.

pair.left: Arnold Toynbee called the Muqaddimah "the greatest work of its kind", and readers from Ernest Gellner to Ronald Reagan said it anticipated modern social science, political theory and economics.
pair.right: Robert Irwin said Ibn Khaldun was a 14th-century Muslim jurist, almost certainly a Sufi, who believed sorcery was real, and that modern admirers had remade him in their own image.

reading.label: The Stakes
reading.text: Both camps say they read him as he was; at stake is whose authority the Muqaddimah lends: a secular science of power seeking an ancestor, or the Islamic learning that produced it.

entries.author: Arx
entries.title: King John Seals Magna Carta at Runnymede
entries.dek: On 15 June 1215 rebel barons force King John to seal a Great Charter at a Thames meadow. Its clauses on lawful judgment and limits on arbitrary rule become England's template for constitutional restraint.

pair.left: Sir Edward Coke and later lawyers treated Magna Carta as the foundation of English liberty against arbitrary kings, and Lord Denning called it the greatest constitutional document of all time.
pair.right: J. C. Holt and later historians said the 1215 charter was a feudal peace deal among barons and a king, and that the story of universal rights was invented centuries afterward.

reading.label: The Stakes
reading.text: Both camps still quote the same parchment; at stake is whether Magna Carta binds as living liberty law or as a medieval settlement remade by later politics.

entries.author: Arx
entries.title: Crusaders Sack Béziers and the Cathar War Begins
entries.dek: On 22 July 1209 the army Innocent III raised against the Cathars storms Béziers and kills Catholics and heretics alike. Twenty years later Languedoc is bound to the French crown.

pair.left: The legate Arnaud Amalric told Innocent III that the crusaders spared no one in Béziers, put almost 20,000 to the sword, and that divine vengeance raged against the city.
pair.right: Raymond Roger Trencavel, viscount of Béziers, said he was a loyal member of the Church and, being young, not to blame for the heresy in his lands.

reading.label: The Stakes
reading.text: Each side said it stood with the Church; at stake was who would rule Languedoc and police its faith, the pope's legates and northern barons or the southern lords.
